text: You time a serial run at \(T_{\mathrm{serial} }\) and the parallel run at \(T_{\mathrm{parallel} }\). Speedup is \(S = {{c1::T_{\mathrm{serial} }/T_{\mathrm{parallel} } }}\).
extra: Ideal case with equal work and no overhead is linear speedup \(S = p\).

text: You fire \(p\) cores, split the work evenly, and add no extra coordination. That dream run hits linear speedup: \(S = {{c1::p}}\).
extra: Best possible: work split evenly and no parallel overhead.

text: Efficiency asks how much of the ideal you kept: \(E = {{c1::S/p}} = {{c2::T_{\mathrm{serial} }/(p \cdot T_{\mathrm{parallel} }) }}\).
extra: Read it as the average fraction of parallel run-time each core spends on the original problem.

text: Add more processes and efficiency \(E = S/p\) usually {{c1::falls}}, because you spend more time on coordination and messaging.
extra: Typical overheads: critical sections, mutexes, network messages, thread management, file I/O. Those make \(S\) a smaller fraction of ideal \(p\).

text: Amdahl with serial fraction \(a\): the parallelizable chunk \(1-a\) scales by \(p\), so \(S = {{c1::1/((1-a)/p + a) }}\).
extra: The textbook also writes the same serial fraction as \(r\). Perfect scaling of \(1-a\) is the assumption.

text: Under Amdahl, pile on infinite cores and speedup still caps at \(S \to {{c1::1/a}}\), where \(a\) is the serial fraction.
extra: Extra cores cannot shrink the serial remainder. Same idea with textbook \(r\): \(S \le 1/r\).

text: You parallelize 90% of a program perfectly, so the serial fraction is \(a = 0.1\). Amdahl says speedup never beats {{c1::10}}.
extra: Limit is \(1/a = 10\), even with thousands of cores.

text: Practice: serial time 100 s, parallel time 40 s on 4 cores. Then \(S = {{c1::2.5}}\) and \(E = {{c2::0.625}}\).
Practice: same 100 s serial job finishes in 25 s on 8 cores. Now \(S = {{c1::4}}\) and \(E = {{c2::0.5}}\).
extra: Versus 4 cores (\(S = 2.5\), \(E = 0.625\)): speedup rose but efficiency fell. Classic overhead-with-\(p\) pattern from study-guide Q5.

text: Split the work evenly, then add overhead, and the parallel time is \(T_{\mathrm{parallel} } = {{c1::T_{\mathrm{serial} }/p + T_{\mathrm{overhead} } }}\).
extra: Then \(E\) is the fraction of parallel run-time spent on the original problem. The rest is overhead.
